item.content:encoded: Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round. The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied all projections to win an unprecedented fourth term at the helm of Latin America’s largest country. According to official results, he won 51.75 percentof the votes to 48.25 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who had entered election day confident with his lead in the polls. With Lula’s victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries — such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru — all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump. After a campaign marred by scandal and mud-slinging, Sunday’s vote plunged into chaos after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extending voting by two hours, at the request of Lula who said buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting. Supporters of Brazil’s President and Workers’ Party (PT) re-election candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva react to the presidential runoff election results in the state of Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 25, 2026. Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on October 25, 2026, as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round. (Photo by NELSON ALMEIDA / AFP) Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some parts of the country due to heavy rains, but his camp lashed out at the country-wide extension. “Either we win. Or we win. Consider yourself warned,” pro-Bolsonaro lawmaker Nikolas Ferreira wrote on X as the votes streamed in. The bitter campaign laid bare the deep divisions in the country of over 200 million people. “It’s a disgrace. We’ve never had anything like this in Brazil, and now they’ve come up with the idea of extending the election period by two hours,” said Aurelio Junior, 45, a dentist in Brasilia. Jacqueline Maria Lima de Franca, 34, a business owner in Rio de Janeiro backing Lula said it was “more than fair…everyone should have the right to vote, and that was being neglected.” – Lula rises from the ashes, again – Lula, a defining figure in Brazilian politics over four decades, was blindsided after his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro. The left swung into action with massive rallies declaring “Never Again Bolsonaro,” where protesters recalled the former president’s chaotic handling of the Covid pandemic, devastation of the Amazon rainforest and cuts to public programs. Lula also revamped his social media strategy, taking video selfies and even bought his first cellphone, while supporters carried out a feverish campaign to change the minds of family, friends and neighbors, and encourage them to vote after high levels of abstention. His re-election marks another remarkable comeback for the man who grew up dirt poor in the northeast in a family of illiterate farmers. Lula, revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months. The charges, annulled on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him. In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but voters complain about the cost of living and a sense of insecurity. Lula’s social policies became a point of tension as he expanded welfare programs during the campaign. “Brazil needs more time with Lula, primarily because the country is on the verge of falling into the clutches of fascism,” Maria Fernanda Elisbao, a 21-year-old editorial assistant, told AFP. – A tricky term ahead – Lula heads into a fourth term with a country divided, with almost half of the nation voting against him and desperate for change. “We’re in a deep hole, things are dire. People can barely afford to eat — buying meat is out of the question,” said Tereza Cristina Ramos, a 68-year-old retiree, who voted in Rio de Janeiro. Already one of the world’s oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030. He will thus have spent 16 years in power, following his first stint as president from 2003 to 2010. Lula is also facing a hostile Congress dominated by the right. His options are also constrained by the economic outlook, with growth expected to slow. He has also come under renewed pressure to confront rampant insecurity in a country plagued by criminal factions that sow terror in working-class neighborhoods. The president’s campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump’s United States. Voters must “choose a country where the flag is respected,” he said, his raspy voice more hoarse than ever after a tireless campaign. item.description: By ANTHONY OGBEIFUN As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general election, the country stands again at a familiar crossroads: the choice between narrow, sectional calculation and the broader national demand for justice, fairness and peace. Elections are not merely contests for power. In a plural society such as Nigeria, they are also referendums on whether citizens believe the state belongs to all of them. Few Nigerian voices expressed this truth more memorably than the late elder statesman and Dan Masanin Kano, Alhaji Yusuf Maitama Sule. In May 2015, Sule led a delegation of the Northern Leaders Forum to congratulate then President-elect Muhammadu Buhari. His counsel on that occasion remains strikingly relevant today. Sule told Buhari: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.” It was a simple statement, but one carrying the weight of Nigeria’s history. The country’s recurrent crises—ethnic suspicion, religious tension, electoral violence, insecurity, economic exclusion and the erosion of public trust—are not disconnected accidents. They are symptoms of a deeper disorder: the feeling among many citizens that fairness is selective, opportunity is unequal and power is used to reward loyalty rather than serve the common good. Sule understood this. “Behind every crisis anywhere in the world is injustice,” he said. Justice, in the sense Sule meant it, is broader than court judgments or legal technicalities. It includes fair representation, equitable distribution of public resources, respect for the rule of law, protection of minorities, credible elections and equal treatment before public institutions. It means that a farmer in Zamfara, a trader in Onitsha, a teacher in Lagos, a fisherman in Bayelsa and a herder in Sokoto should all be able to expect the state to protect their lives, respect their rights and respond to their needs without discrimination. Sule put it plainly: “If you do justice to all and sundry — and I say all and sundry — because Allah says, ‘If you are going to judge between two people, do justice irrespective of the tribe, religion or even political inclination; justice must be done to whosoever deserves it.’” That standard is demanding. It rejects the politics of “our turn” when it becomes a cover for exclusion. It also rejects the politics of revenge, where one group’s victory is treated as another group’s defeat. Nigeria needs leaders who can rise above such thinking. The late Dan Masanin Kano was equally clear that justice must not be selective. “I am not asking you — and I know you will not — to discriminate against any part of Nigeria,” he told Buhari. “But I am asking you to do justice to all parts of Nigeria.” For political parties preparing for 2027, fairness must begin before the first ballot is cast. It must be visible in candidate selection, zoning arrangements, internal party democracy, campaign financing and the treatment of aspirants. When parties manipulate primaries, impose candidates, marginalise women and young people, or allow money to determine nomination, they weaken the legitimacy of the eventual winner. A flawed process produces a fragile mandate. And a fragile mandate makes governing harder, especially in a country where citizens are already sceptical of political promises. Fairness also requires issue-based campaigns. Nigeria’s problems are real: insecurity, unemployment, inflation, poor infrastructure, weak public services, climate pressure on agriculture and widespread poverty. These challenges do not respect ethnicity or religion. Candidates should therefore be judged on their plans to secure communities, create jobs, reform institutions, expand opportunities and restore public confidence. A campaign built on fear, sectional resentment or religious division may win attention, but it cannot build a nation. Sule’s warning remains urgent: force, fear and power cannot govern the mind or conquer the spirit. Only justice and fair play can. Sule linked justice directly to peace and development. “Justice will bring about peace,” he said. “Peace and stability are the pre-requisites of development.” No society develops sustainably in an atmosphere of fear. Investors hesitate where contracts are uncertain and violence is common. Farmers abandon land where insecurity prevails. Young people lose hope where merit is ignored and corruption rewards the connected. Communities retreat into distrust when they believe the state protects some citizens more than others. Peace is not merely the absence of gunfire. It is the presence of confidence: confidence that elections will count, that courts will be impartial, that public offices will serve the public, and that no region, faith or class will be permanently shut out of opportunity. The 2027 election offers Nigeria a chance to rebuild that confidence. But it will require more than campaign rhetoric. It will require electoral institutions that are visibly independent, security agencies that act professionally, political actors who accept results peacefully, and citizens who refuse to be used as instruments of violence. Nigeria does not lack talent, resources or ideas. What it often lacks is the disciplined commitment to justice that turns diversity into strength rather than division. Maitama Sule’s message was not addressed to one president alone. It was addressed to every Nigerian leader, in every generation, and to every citizen who hopes for a better country. As 2027 approaches, voters should ask hard questions: Which candidate will uphold the rule of law even when it is inconvenient? Which party will distribute opportunity fairly? Which leader will govern for all Nigerians, not merely for those who funded a campaign or share a regional identity? The answer should not be based on sentiment, ethnicity or fear. It should be based on justice. Sule’s counsel remains a compass: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.” If Nigeria’s political class embraces that key, the 2027 election can become more than another contest for office. It can become a renewal of the national promise—a step towards a country at peace with itself, fair to all its people, and capable at last of fulfilling its vast potential. •Ogbeifun wrote in from Lagos. item.title: Making gas operations safer
item.description: Nigeria’s ambition to expand the use of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) must be matched by a serious commitment to safety. The Nigerian Association of Liquefied Petroleum Gas Marketers (NALPGAM), at its recent webinar on operational excellence and compliance, warned that rising consumption alone cannot guarantee a sustainable industry. Every facility must be safe, every operator competent, every process compliant and every customer protected. The warning is timely. LPG offers households and businesses a cleaner alternative to firewood, charcoal and other polluting fuels, but it is highly flammable. Leaking gas, overfilled cylinders, defective valves, poorly maintained equipment and unsafe storage can turn premises into disaster scenes. Illegal decanting and unauthorised propane blending compound these risks, endangering workers, consumers and neighbouring communities. Such practices must not be treated as commercial shortcuts. NALPGAM’s proposed Standard of Operational Excellence, built around safe facilities, trained personnel, compliant processes and consumer protection, deserves support. But a declaration is not enforcement. The association must translate its aspiration into measurable obligations for members, while the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) must sustain inspections, investigate violations and apply sanctions. Operators should maintain equipment, verify cylinder integrity, provide fire and gas-detection systems, and report incidents promptly. Regulators should publish inspection and enforcement data so the public can judge progress. Technology can strengthen this effort. Smart filling systems, calibrated load cells, flow meters, automated tank gauges and vehicle tracking can improve measurement, trace product movements and expose losses or suspicious transactions. Digital tools, however, are no substitute for trained staff, independent checks and functioning emergency procedures. Small operators may need affordable training, technical guidance and finance for compliant upgrades; such assistance must never become an excuse to relax minimum safety standards. Safety also has an economic dimension. Accidents destroy lives, property, investment and public confidence. Consumers who fear explosions or suspect short-changing may avoid cooking gas, frustrating efforts to broaden its use. item.title: When a police officer is caught at crime scene
item.description: By Owolola Adebola The sight of a police officer at a crime scene should ordinarily inspire confidence, reassurance and hope. It should signal the arrival of law, the protection of innocent citizens and the beginning of justice for victims. But what happens when the very officer expected to prevent a crime is caught participating in it? What happens when the uniform that should represent honour becomes a disguise for criminality? At that moment, the incident transcends the conduct of an individual officer. It becomes a test of the integrity of the police institution, the effectiveness of internal supervision and the willingness of the state to hold its own agents accountable. A police officer caught at a crime scene under suspicious circumstances presents a troubling contradiction. The law enforcement agent who should be chasing criminals may suddenly find himself on the other side of the law. The individual entrusted with protecting lives and property may become a threat to the very people whose safety he has sworn to defend. Such an incident demands serious investigation, not institutional excuses. Of course, insanity creeps in when the uniform becomes a shield for criminality because the police uniform carries authority. It commands attention, opens doors and gives its wearer powers that ordinary citizens do not possess. These privileges are granted for public service, not personal enrichment, intimidation or criminal enterprise. Unfortunately, when an officer abuses that authority, the consequences can be devastating. A police officer involved in robbery, kidnapping, extortion, unlawful possession of weapons or the protection of criminal gangs does more than violate the law. He exploits public confidence and undermines the institution he represents. The situation becomes even more disturbing when an officer is found at a scene where criminal activities are taking place and credible evidence suggests that he may be involved. Rather than automatically treating the officer as guilty, the authorities must establish what brought him there, what role he played and whether his presence was lawful. A family whose relative has been victimised by an officer may lose faith in the complaint process. A community that repeatedly encounters alleged police misconduct may begin to regard law enforcement as a source of danger rather than protection. This erosion of trust gives criminals additional room to operate. Witnesses become reluctant to speak, victims withdraw complaints and valuable intelligence disappears into a climate of suspicion. The damage is not limited to the immediate victims. Honest police officers also pay the price. Their sacrifices, courage and commitment can be overshadowed by the misconduct of colleagues who betray the institution. It is therefore in the interest of the police themselves to confront criminality within their ranks decisively. Protecting a compromised officer does not protect the institution; it places the reputation of the entire force at risk. In a way, investigation must replace cover-up. Whenever a police officer is apprehended at a crime scene under circumstances suggesting criminal involvement, the first responsibility of the authorities is to establish the facts. Rank, seniority, political connections and years of service must not determine whether an investigation proceeds. item.title: We never left Egypt, only prodigals need to return home, by Owei Lakemfa
item.description: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu told Nigerians on October 19, 2026, that they will not return to Egypt. He seems unaware that Egypt is our ancestral home and that we never left and will never leave. This Niger Area is the land of milk and honey we inherited from our fathers and mothers. We were never slaves in this land, will fight any attempt to enslave us; therefore, we never had any reason to flee. We never had any reason to part ways with the sea or for the sea to part ways for us. We never needed to wander in any desert for forty years or more, seeking pathways to freedom or prosperity. This has never been, and will never be, our portion in life. Ancient Egypt is the origin of modern civilisation. It civilised the Greeks and Romans, who were its pupils before they passed that civilisation to the rest of Europe. The peoples who make up Nigeria were self-sufficient, with viable city-states and empires, and well-schooled in their non-Western education. One of the natural endowments of this beautiful country is oil. We began producing it in commercial quantities from 1956–57. We were self-sufficient in it, including local refining, with the country running four refineries. As then Head of State Yakubu Gowon said in 1973: “Money is not Nigeria’s problem, but how to spend it.” What has happened to Nigeria is not that oil has stopped flowing. It is not that the technology to refine sufficient petroleum products for local consumption and export has been lost. Rather, the tragedy we face is that we have had a mainly prodigal leadership since military rule began sixty years ago. So, in our Egypt, we have sufficient oil reserves that will last at least the next sixty years. There was no fuel subsidy because we did not need to subsidise what we have. It is like asking a rich farmer with fertile soil and bursting barns of yam to subsidise the pounded yam his family will have for supper. What has happened is that a prodigal political class took over, deliberately ran down the refineries, refused to build new ones and, most criminally, insisted on denominating fuel in inflated dollar accounting. item.content:encoded: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu told Nigerians on October 19, 2026, that they will not return to Egypt. He seems unaware that Egypt is our ancestral home and that we never left and will never leave. This Niger Area is the land of milk and honey we inherited from our fathers and mothers. We were never slaves in this land, will fight any attempt to enslave us; therefore, we never had any reason to flee. We never had any reason to part ways with the sea or for the sea to part ways for us. We never needed to wander in any desert for forty years or more, seeking pathways to freedom or prosperity. This has never been, and will never be, our portion in life. Ancient Egypt is the origin of modern civilisation. It civilised the Greeks and Romans, who were its pupils before they passed that civilisation to the rest of Europe. The peoples who make up Nigeria were self-sufficient, with viable city-states and empires, and well-schooled in their non-Western education. One of the natural endowments of this beautiful country is oil. We began producing it in commercial quantities from 1956–57. We were self-sufficient in it, including local refining, with the country running four refineries. As then Head of State Yakubu Gowon said in 1973: “Money is not Nigeria’s problem, but how to spend it.” What has happened to Nigeria is not that oil has stopped flowing. It is not that the technology to refine sufficient petroleum products for local consumption and export has been lost. Rather, the tragedy we face is that we have had a mainly prodigal leadership since military rule began sixty years ago. So, in our Egypt, we have sufficient oil reserves that will last at least the next sixty years. There was no fuel subsidy because we did not need to subsidise what we have. It is like asking a rich farmer with fertile soil and bursting barns of yam to subsidise the pounded yam his family will have for supper. What has happened is that a prodigal political class took over, deliberately ran down the refineries, refused to build new ones and, most criminally, insisted on denominating fuel in inflated dollar accounting. Their paper accounting is based on our country having no drop of oil, which we all know is false, and having to import finished products which are bought by dubious officials from their chosen partners, pay freight, insurance, port fees, demurrage and storage fees. These products are then handed over to a cartel which transports them through deliberately neglected or abandoned roads and sells them to hapless Nigerians at rates imposed by the cartel. In this dubious process is built what is touted as subsidy. Since the Babangida regime, this dubious subsidy mirage has been factored into our petroleum products. When the latest subsidy removal was touted on May 29, 2023, Nigerians were told the proceeds would be used for development. But what we have experienced is greater misery, multiplication of the hungry, dilapidating infrastructure, a rising number of out-of-school children, lack of mass housing, virtually abandoned basic healthcare and insecurity. Whenever we ask the administration what has been done with the so-called subsidy savings, it points at increasing the revenue allocation to states and local governments. It is aware that most leaders of these tiers are like cats being told to watch over fried fish. Deceptively, it does not point at itself as being the largest recipient of these extra funds, which remain unaccounted for. When President Tinubu announced that his administration had removed fuel subsidy, the price of a litre of PMS was increased from about N197 to an average N500. Today, it is thrice that price, and the government blames this insanity on the war in Iran. In this, the Tinubu government is behaving like the dirty widow with head lice creeping all over her hair who blames this on mourning her husband by not allowing a drop of water to touch her head since his demise. If the Nigerian government blames the war in Iran for the outrageous price of PMS in the country, why is Iran, which has suffered the catastrophe of having its leadership wiped out, children buried under the rubble of their classrooms, infrastructure and oil facilities bombed and punishing sanctions imposed by the United States, not been similarly affected? Honourable Victor Afam Oghene, Member, Federal House of Representatives, Ogbaru Constituency of Anambra State, debunked, with verifiable statistics, these childish fairy tales of the Tinubu government. He gave comparative statistics of PMS prices in four oil-producing countries: Iran, which has been at war for years; Libya, which has suffered state collapse since 2011 and had at least three factional governments in Tobruk, Tripoli and Benghazi; Saudi Arabia, which is engaged in war with neighbouring Yemen; and Nigeria, which is not at war. In his statistics, which the increasingly intolerant Tinubu government and its army of internet propagandists have not been able to fault, Honourable Oghene revealed that a litre of PMS in Iran is N38, Libya, N32, Saudi Arabia, N832, and Nigeria, at least N1,300. In contrast, the National Minimum Wage in Iran is N165,000, Libya is N210,000, Saudi Arabia, N1.4 million, and N70,000 in Nigeria! Oghene then analysed these basic statistics in value terms. He showed that the minimum wage in Iran can purchase 4,242 litres of PMS, Libya, 6,562 litres, Saudi Arabia, 1,700, and only 46 litres in Nigeria! Tragically, despite such sound analysis and the situation in the country, the Tinubu administration appears increasingly irritated, deaf to the cries of Nigerians and incapable of basic thinking. For instance, rather than examine the arguments of various patriots and pro-people activists on the issue of fuel subsidy and the calamitous effects on the populace, it is threatening Nigerians with dire consequences. In its unfathomable scare-mongering, the administration’s Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, threatened that even an inkling of the administration rethinking the subsidy issue would trigger capital flight. This, he claimed, would lead to the naira, which has already been devalued over fifty per cent by Tinubu, suffering a further sixty per cent devaluation. Oyedele told Nigerians this fable, not based on any analysis, but beliefs. He also claimed that this would raise the price of petrol to at least N2,000 per litre. Even as a product of Yale University and London School of Economics, and an advertised policy expert, the Honourable Minister could not provide the cost component of this his projected N2,000-per-litre PMS. We Nigerians never left our Egypt, so there is no issue of a return. It is the prodigals of the political class that need to return home, ask for forgiveness and stop suffocating the country. For Africa, these demands coincide with a pressing need to expand electricity access, industrialise economies and create productive employment. The challenge is not simply to defend the relevance of hydrocarbons, but to demonstrate that African energy resources can be developed competitively, responsibly and profitably. The lessons from Houston offer a practical starting point. Artificial intelligence, advanced reservoir analytics, predictive maintenance, drilling automation and digital production monitoring are creating opportunities to improve oil recovery, reduce equipment failures, shorten operational delays and strengthen investment decisions. Their significance lies not in technological novelty, but in their potential to improve the economics of producing assets. Consider Nigeria’s mature oilfields, many of which face declining production, ageing infrastructure, rising water cuts and expensive maintenance requirements. Better integration of geological data, well-performance records and production information can help operators identify underperforming wells, prioritise interventions and determine where additional investment is most likely to recover lost production. Predictive maintenance can similarly help operators identify early warning signs in pumps, compressors and other critical equipment before failures cause costly shutdowns. Improved drilling analytics can support better well planning, reduce non-productive time and strengthen operational safety. Meanwhile, methane monitoring and flare-management technologies can help operators identify emissions sources, reduce avoidable losses and improve environmental performance. These are practical applications for Nigeria’s oil and gas industry, not automatic outcomes of technology adoption. Results depend on reliable data, competent personnel, appropriate infrastructure and disciplined implementation. Every investment should therefore be assessed against measurable indicators, including incremental production, reduced downtime, lower operating costs, improved recovery and emissions reduction. This approach is particularly important as Nigeria’s upstream industry undergoes structural change. The transfer of selected onshore and shallow-water assets from international oil companies to indigenous operators has created opportunities for domestic companies to expand their participation and retain more value within the economy. Yet a change of ownership does not automatically produce higher output, stronger profitability or sustainable operations. Indigenous operators must combine ownership with the technical and financial capacity to manage complex reservoirs, rehabilitate infrastructure, improve recovery and meet environmental obligations. Access to technology, long-term financing, specialised engineering expertise and dependable evacuation systems will be critical to their success. Nigeria’s ambition to achieve three million barrels of crude oil production per day by 2030 must therefore be treated as an execution challenge rather than a statement of intent. New developments, improved recovery from existing fields, reduced production losses, reliable evacuation and sustained investment must work together to deliver the desired outcome. The leadership transition within the SPE Nigeria Council, from Engr. Francis Nwaochei to Engr. Etta Agbor, also presents an opportunity to strengthen the connection between global technical knowledge and local operating realities. Professional institutions such as SPE can support this process through applied research, technical training, industry collaboration and the development of Nigerian engineering talent capable of evaluating and deploying advanced technologies. However, technology alone cannot overcome an uncertain investment environment. Regulatory predictability remains fundamental. The Petroleum Industry Act provides an important statutory framework, but investors also require transparent fiscal arrangements, timely approvals, consistent regulatory decisions and clarity over contractual obligations. Effective regulation should protect public interests while enabling commercially viable projects to proceed without avoidable administrative delays. Security and infrastructure are equally important. Production cannot generate its full economic value if crude oil and gas cannot reach markets reliably. Pipeline disruptions, theft, infrastructure failures and insecurity increase operating costs, undermine revenues and weaken investor confidence. Government institutions, regulators, operators, security agencies and host communities must work together to protect infrastructure and strengthen the reliability of Nigeria’s energy supply chain. Environmental performance is also becoming integral to commercial competitiveness. Methane detection, flare reduction, emissions monitoring and environmental remediation increasingly influence investor assessments and access to international financing. Operators must incorporate these responsibilities into field-development plans and operating budgets rather than treating them as separate sustainability commitments. item.description: ‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru PRESIDENT Bola Tinubu has extended his heartfelt condolences to the Okonjo royal family of Ogwashi-Uku, Delta State, on the passing of Prof. Kamene Okonjo, who died at the age of 96. Prof. Okonjo was a distinguished scholar, a champion of women’s empowerment, and a revered matriarch. The President particularly commiserated with her daughter, Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Director-General of the World Trade Organisation, other family members, and the people of Ogwashi-Uku over the loss of their beloved mother, matriarch, and community leader. President Tinubu described Prof. Okonjo’s passing as the loss of an accomplished academic whose life was defined by intellectual distinction, service to humanity, and an enduring commitment to advancing women and society. item.title: Soldiers earn peanuts, APC youth leader flaunts billion-naira SUVs — Utomi
item.description: Professor Pat Utomi has criticised the All Progressives Congress (APC) over the distribution of luxury sport utility vehicles (SUVs) to selected youth leaders, contrasting the expenditure with what he described as poor salaries paid to Nigerian soldiers. Utomi, a chieftain of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), said it was troubling that an APC youth leader could display expensive vehicles at a time Nigerians had been told that government funds were limited. In a post on X on Sunday, Utomi wrote: “Nigerian soldiers are being paid peanuts as salaries, yet an APC youth leader is flaunting SUVs worth billions of naira. This is the same government that told Nigerians there was no longer money in the treasury. At this point, they must think we are fools!” In another post, the professor questioned whether the money spent on the vehicles could have been put to better use, particularly in the health sector. “Each of the SUVs in this video costs more than ₦100 million. I wonder how many world-class ambulances the millions being spent on these vehicles could buy. What a pity!” he wrote. The comments followed a video posted by APC National Youth Leader, Dayo Israel, showing brand-new 2026 Toyota Prado SUVs he said were presented to selected youth leaders to support election mobilisation ahead of the 2027 general elections. “Today, I presented brand new 2026 Prado to my committed selected youth leaders to aid their election mobilisation activities,” Israel wrote. He also expressed gratitude to First Lady Oluremi Tinubu for what he described as her continued support for the party’s structure under his leadership. “The party is supreme and that supremacy will show in our action in this election period — we will deliver polling unit by polling unit,” he added. The video, which has since been deleted, drew criticism from Nigerians on social media, with some questioning the timing of the vehicle distribution amid the economic hardship associated with the Tinubu administration’s reforms. Utomi’s remarks add to the criticism surrounding the display, with the NDC chieftain raising questions about public spending priorities and the cost of the vehicles. item.title: Ebola: Lagos Intensifies Surveillance, Reassures Residents Of Preparedness
item.description: The Lagos State Government has said it is ready to prevent, detect and respond to potential public health threats, amid concerns over the confirmation of Nigeria’s first case of the Bundibugyo virus in the Federal Capital Territory. It urged residents and visitors not to panic, as the Ministry of Health, through the Directorate of Epidemiology, Biosecurity and Global Health, is strengthening disease surveillance, risk communication and community engagement, as well as collaboration with agencies at points of entry, including the Murtala Muhammed International Airport (MMIA), to enhance early detection and response to suspected cases. item.description: Daniel Bwala, an aide to President Bola Tinubu, has criticised the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) over its National Campaign Council for the 2027 general elections, describing the list as being “filled with content creators”. Bwala, in a post on X shortly after the party announced the council on Sunday, also accused the NDC of concealing the identities of its media surrogates in mainstream media. “@PeterObi and NDC have released their list of campaign council members; and as expected it is filled with content creators,” he wrote. “They stylishly refused to name their campaign media surrogates in the mainstream media masquerading as OAP.” @PeterObi and NDC have released their list of campaign council members; and as expected it is filled with content creators. They stylishly refused to name their campaign media surrogates in the mainstream media masquerading as OAP. — D. H Bwala (@BwalaDaniel) October 25, 2026 The NDC had earlier announced the constitution of its National Campaign Council, saying it would coordinate campaign activities nationwide and mobilise support for its candidates ahead of the 2027 elections. Under the arrangement, the party’s National Leader, Senator Henry Seriake Dickson, will serve as chairman, while its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, will be co-chairman. The party’s National Chairman, Senator Cleopas Moses Zuwoghe, was named vice-chairman, while its vice-presidential candidate, Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, will serve as co-vice-chairman. The NDC’s National Secretary, Barrister Ikenna Morgan Enekweizu, was named council secretary, while Mallam Ibrahim Hussain Abdulkarim will serve as director-general. Announcing the council, the party said it would provide “strategic leadership” and drive nationwide mobilisation behind its vision of “a new, just, and prosperous Nigeria”. The NDC also said the council would deliver a “people-centred and issue-based campaign” and urged its members, supporters and other Nigerians to remain united ahead of the elections. Bwala’s comments came shortly after the announcement, as political parties prepare their structures and mobilisation strategies for the 2027 general elections. item.title: 2027: NDC releases campaign council list, names Dickson chairman, Obi co-chair
item.description: The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has named its National Leader, Senator Henry Seriake Dickson, as chairman of its National Campaign Council for the 2027 general elections, with its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, as co-chairman. The party said the council would work towards delivering a campaign focused on the needs of Nigerians and policy issues. It described its proposed campaign as “people-centred and issue-based”, while urging party members and supporters to remain united ahead of the 2027 elections. “We call on all party members, supporters, and well-meaning Nigerians to remain united and focused as we work together to rescue our country,” the NDC said. The announcement comes as political parties begin preparations for the 2027 general elections, with campaigns expected to focus on candidates, policy proposals and nationwide mobilisation. item.title: Opebi-Mende-Ojota Link Bridge To Be Opened Before Christmas, Says Sanwo-Olu
item.description: The Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu has said that the Opebi-Mende Link Bridge is about 80 per cent complete, expressing confidence that the project will be opened to the public before Christmas. Governor Sanwo-Olu gave the assurance during an inspection of the project, acknowledging that the construction had exceeded the September completion timeline previously announced. He said his visit to the site was to establish the reasons for the delay and assess the progress of work, stressing that the project’s distinctive architectural design and engineering requirements must not be compromised by the pressure to meet the deadline. He explained that the bridge’s steel structure was designed to reflect the area’s historical association with cane weaving, thereby preserving its cultural identity. According to him, the project involves installing more than 300 tonnes of steel at heights of up to 25 metres, making it an unusually demanding engineering undertaking. The governor said three of the four major steel components, designed to resemble interwoven cane, had been completed, while work was ongoing on the remaining component. He added that light-emitting diode (LED) installations featuring the colours of Lagos State would enhance the structure and give it an iconic appearance. Governor Sanwo-Olu added that the state government would not sacrifice engineering quality and public safety for speed, despite the delay. He said additional activities, including site cleaning, repainting of kerbs, restoration of affected areas and landscaping, would be undertaken before the bridge is opened to the public. He envisaged the area becoming a destination for recreation, cultural heritage and tourism, adding that its redevelopment would enable residents to appreciate the history and identity of the community. The governor maintained that the bridge would become a significant infrastructure landmark in Lagos, combining innovation with cultural preservation. Sanwo-Olu commissioned the construction of the bridge in 2022 to ease congestion in Ikeja and environs. Governor Sanwo-Olu (centre) He said that the bridge, which is part of the ‘legacy project,’ was an innovative solution to the perennial gridlock around Opebi/Mobolaji Bank Anthony Way/Ojota/Mende corridor. item.description: Bayern Munich reclaimed top spot in the Bundesliga with a 3-1 win at Freiburg on Sunday, days after coach Vincent Kompany was hospitalised when he collapsed at training. Kompany remains in hospital and is being treated for a mystery virus, with Bayern saying Saturday the coach is likely to be out for “days, not weeks”. “I just opened my phone to a message from Vince saying ‘well done’ and he was happy,” assistant coach Aaron Danks told DAZN. “I just replied saying ‘brilliant — now go rest’. I sent him a kissing emoji, so hopefully he rests up.” Bayern sporting director Max Eberl gave an update on Kompany’s condition. “He’s stable. He no longer has a headache. He’s now undergoing a thorough examination. Everything is being handled,” he said. “There’s no diagnosis, nothing final yet.” With victory Bayern leapfrogged Borussia Dortmund to top the table ahead of the duo’s clash in Munich next week. item.title: 2027: Keyamo to lead APC presidential campaign air operations
item.description: By Dickson Omobola President Bola Tinubu has appointed Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, to head the Directorate of Air Mobilisation of the All Progressives Congress, APC, 2027 re-election campaign Keyamo would serve as Director of the Directorate of Air Mobilisation, with the Managing Director of the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria, FAAN, Mrs Olubunmi Kuku, appointed Deputy Director 1, while Engr Farouk Ahmed Umar would serve as Deputy Director II. Special Adviser on Media and Communications to the Minister, Tunde Moshood, in a statement, said the appointments underscored the strategic importance of air transportation, operational coordination and aviation logistics to the organisation of a nationwide presidential campaign in a country as geographically extensive as Nigeria. The statement reads: ‘The Directorate of Air Mobilisation is expected to play a crucial role in coordinating the campaign’s air-movement requirements, facilitating travel arrangements for designated campaign officials and personnel, and ensuring effective planning for air transportation in support of campaign activities across the six geopolitical zones of the country. “Given the scale of the 2027 presidential campaign, the directorate is expected to work closely with other relevant campaign structures to promote seamless coordination, operational efficiency and effective deployment of available logistical resources, subject to applicable aviation regulations and electoral laws. “Keyamo’s appointment brings to the campaign structure the experience of a serving aviation minister who has been at the forefront of policy initiatives aimed at strengthening Nigeria’s aviation sector, improving its international standing and positioning the country as a major aviation hub in Africa. “His familiarity with the operational demands of the aviation industry is expected to provide useful leadership in coordinating the directorate’s activities and establishing an effective framework for air-mobilisation planning. “The appointment of Mrs. Olubunmi Kuku and Umar as Deputy Directors also brings aviation-sector leadership and technical experience into the directorate, strengthening its capacity to address the planning and coordination demands associated with nationwide campaign movements.” The post 2027: Keyamo to lead APC presidential campaign air operations appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Police Foil Railway Vandalism, Arrest Four Suspects With 70 Stolen Sleepers In Katsina
item.description: The Katsina State Police Command has arrested four suspected railway vandals and recovered 70 railway sleepers believed to have been stolen. The suspects were apprehended on October 11, 2026, at about 12:30 a.m., when police operatives on routine stop-and-search duty along the Kurfi–Tsanni Village Road intercepted a white J5 vehicle. The vehicle, driven by a 25-year-old man, was said to be carrying three other occupants. A thorough search of the vehicle uncovered 70 railway sleepers carefully concealed behind 17 bags of animal feed in what investigators believe was an attempt to evade detection. Police said preliminary investigations revealed that one of the suspects confessed to receiving the railway materials from a suspected supplier from Bauchi State, who is currently at large. The police said 70 railway sleepers were carefully concealed behind 17 bags of animal feed in what investigators believe was an attempt to evade detection. According to the police command, the stolen items were being transported for delivery to a man in Katsina. It said that the four suspects are currently in police custody, while the operational vehicle, the recovered railway sleepers and the bags of animal feed used to conceal them have been secured as exhibits. The Command said efforts are underway to apprehend the fleeing suspects and determine the exact location from which the railway infrastructure was vandalised, adding that investigations are ongoing. In a statement issued on Sunday, the Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Abubakar Sadiq, described the arrests as another breakthrough in the fight against crimes targeting critical national infrastructure. Sadiq said the Commissioner of Police, CP Ali Umar Fage, reaffirmed the Command’s unwavering commitment to protecting critical national infrastructure and bringing perpetrators of vandalism to justice. The PPRO said that the commissioner also appealed to residents to continue supporting security agencies with timely and credible information that will enable the police to prevent crime and swiftly apprehend criminal elements across the state.
